title: The stages
hook: a whole path laid out like a staircase, and an early step is noticing you're alive

segments.voice: Yesterday, lojong, the slogans. Your line was drive all blames into one. Did you catch the mind building a case? This week ran from watching things change, to calm, to silent retreats, to the monk's rule, to the bowl at dawn, to mind training. Today closes the week with a map. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five.
screen: `DRIVE ALL BLAMES INTO ONE.` → `A WEEK OF SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: This map doesn't start with what's wrong with anyone. Before it says a word about meditation or wisdom or awakening, it asks the reader to stop and take stock of something so ordinary it's easy to skip: you woke up today. You have a mind that can learn. You have enough time, right now, to hear a teaching. Tibetan teachers linger here before they move on to anything that sounds more spiritual. The idea is that nobody climbs a staircase without first noticing they're standing at the bottom of one, with legs that work. Today's word is the staircase.
screen: `NOT WHAT'S WRONG.` → `YOU WOKE UP TODAY.` → `THE BOTTOM OF A STAIRCASE.`

segments.voice: Lamrim is Tibetan for stages of the path. It names a way of laying out the whole of the Buddha's teaching in order, step by step, so that each step prepares the next. Tibetan tradition traces it to Atisha, the same teacher behind yesterday's slogans, who wrote a short work called A Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment. Later, the Tibetan teacher Tsongkhapa wrote a great treatise on the stages. Four turns. First, the order matters. In Atisha's Lamp, people are sorted by what they're seeking: some want a better future, some want freedom from suffering for themselves, and some want awakening for the sake of everyone. The path meets each one where they are and leads them up. Second, an early step is precious human life. The teachers list freedoms and good fortunes: being free of conditions that make practice impossible, having a working mind, meeting a teaching. The point is not to feel lucky in a vague way. It's to see the opening clearly. Third, it's rare. The Buddha, in a discourse, gives an image: a yoke with one hole floating on a wide ocean, and a blind turtle that surfaces now and then. The chance that the turtle's head comes up through that hole, he says, is greater than the chance of a human birth for someone lost in the lower realms. Lamrim teachers use the image to say: this life is an unlikely opening. Fourth, it's urgent, but not anxious. If the opening is rare, it's worth using today. The map runs on from here toward compassion and wisdom, and this early step makes the later ones possible.
screen: `A PATH LAID OUT IN ORDER.` · `IT MEETS PEOPLE WHERE THEY ARE.` · `PRECIOUS HUMAN LIFE COMES FIRST.` · `THE BLIND TURTLE AND THE YOKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: consider your precious life. Sit, and let the breath settle. Count, slowly, the openings you have right now. A body that's breathing. A mind that can follow a sentence. A few minutes with nothing urgent. Maybe a person who'd pick up if you called. Don't rush past any of them. Let each one land before you go to the next. If a hard part of your life shows up, it can sit in the room too. Just keep counting openings. The bell holds the time.
Lamrim. The stages of the path in Tibetan Buddhism, a step-by-step map from noticing a precious human life all the way to awakening. Today's word.

Your line: precious human life. Today, once in the afternoon, stop and name one opening you have that you didn't have to earn. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-five, and a week of schools behind you.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, students often study the lamrim in order with a teacher, beginning with contemplation of precious human life, and some recite short lamrim prayers that summarize the whole path.

fork.setup: you're a new student of the lamrim. before meditation techniques or deep philosophy, what does the map ask you to look at first?
fork.reveal: an early step is precious human life: the freedoms and good fortunes that make practice possible at all.

original.note: Tibetan lam rim: stages of the path.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of steps to enlightenment.
what it means: a map of the whole path in order, starting with seeing clearly how rare and open this life is.
what a scholar hears: Atisha's Lamp for the Path, Tsongkhapa's great treatise, and the blind-turtle simile behind precious human life.

notes: Week end: review looks back at days 1359–1364.

The blind turtle simile is from MN 129 (also SN 56.47); the 'once every hundred years' detail was left out. Paraphrase compares the turtle's chance with human rebirth for a being in the lower realms; confirm the paraphrase is faithful.
Three kinds of persons (small, middling, great scope) from Atisha's Lamp are described without the count; confirm.
Freedoms and endowments (the eight freedoms, ten endowments) described without numbers; confirm the plain summary.
Hook says Tibetan teachers 'sometimes' spend days of a retreat on precious human life; confirm or soften.
Hook opening rewritten to avoid a general claim about other books.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'sometimes days of a retreat'; 'the first step' softened to 'an early step' (Lamrim Chenmo puts reliance on the teacher before precious human life); replaced 'begin with gratitude and end with compassion', which misdescribed the lamrim's order, with 'runs on toward compassion and wisdom'.
